claims.evidence: The LED driver for optogenetics is described as an integrated feature

claims.claim: NINscope acquisition and control software is cross-platform compatible
claims.source: User-friendly software was developed in the Processing language (http://processing.org), allowing true cross-platform interoperability and control of experimental recordings (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Software was developed in Processing language which enables cross-platform use

claims.claim: NINscope permits dual site recordings in unrestrained mice
claims.source: Given the reduced footprint and weight of NINscope, we were able to mount two miniscopes on a single mouse (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Experimental demonstration of dual miniscope mounting is described and shown

claims.claim: Mice wearing two NINscopes showed no significant difference in rearing behavior compared to mice wearing one miniscope
claims.source: Both the number of rearings and their duration were unaffected in mice wearing two miniscopes (number of rearings one scope = 1.47 ± 1.07 rearings/min. mean ± SD; number of rearings two scopes: 1.36 ± 0.75 rearings/min. mean ± SD, p=0.7864, n.s.; rearing duration one scope = 2.21 ± 1.11 s mean ± SD; rearing duration two scopes = 1.84 ± 0.77 s mean ± SD, p=0.4244, n.s.; N = 4 mice, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of rearing behavior between single and dual scope conditions

claims.claim: NINscope enables the first concurrent cellular resolution recordings from cerebellum and cerebral cortex in unrestrained mice
claims.source: We use it to perform the first concurrent cellular resolution recordings from cerebellum and cerebral cortex in unrestrained mice, demonstrate its optogenetic stimulation capabilities to examine cerebello-cerebral or cortico-striatal connectivity, and replicate findings of action encoding in dorsal striatum.
claims.evidence: The authors explicitly state this is the first such recording

claims.claim: Event rates measured from Purkinje cell dendrites corresponded to the underlying rate of climbing fiber input
claims.source: Event rates measured from Purkinje cell dendrites corresponded to the underlying rate of climbing fiber input (0.62 ± 0.39 Hz, mean± SD, 1629 cells, N = 4 mice), while cortical neurons fired events at a lower rate (0.22 ± 0.28 Hz, mean ± SD, 2212 cells, N = 4 mice).
claims.evidence: Event rates are measured and compared to known climbing fiber firing rates

claims.claim: Significantly more Purkinje cells participated in across-region synchronous patterns than cortical neurons
claims.source: Significantly more Purkinje cells participated in across-SPs than cortical neurons (fraction of total lobule VI: 42.3 ± 29.6%; fraction simplex lobule: 47.4 ± 31.6%; cortex: 26.7 ± 18.5%, mean ± SD; CBL vs CTX p=1.8409e-15, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of participation rates between brain regions

claims.claim: The majority (86%, 99/115) of synchronous patterns associated with significant acceleration events occurred following the across-region synchronous pattern
claims.source: Thus, the majority (86%, 99/115) of SPs associated with significant acceleration events following the across-SP.
claims.evidence: Temporal relationship between synchronous patterns and acceleration is quantified

claims.claim: Coordinated cerebello-cerebral activity generally precedes peak acceleration of a movement
claims.source: Thus, based on our preliminary data recorded with NINscope, we show that coordinated cerebello-cerebral activity generally precedes peak acceleration of a movement.
claims.evidence: Temporal analysis of calcium transients relative to movement acceleration

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of cerebellar Purkinje cells evoked reflexive movements with delays after stimulus offset (crus II ipsi: 76 ± 23 ms; crus II contra: 80 ± 30 ms; lobule VI: 79 ± 34 ms; simplex lobule: 73 ± 32 ms)
claims.source: The miniscope accelerometer data registered movement that occurred with a delay after stimulus offset (crus II ipsi: 76 ± 23 ms; crus II contra: 80 ± 30 ms; lobule VI: 79 ± 34 ms; simplex lobule: 73 ± 32 ms, mean ± SD, N = 2 mice) in line with earlier observations that disinhibition of Purkinje cells and associated rebound excitation of neurons in the cerebellar nuclei can elicit delayed motor reflexes (Hoebeek et al., 2010; Witter et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Measured delays between optogenetic stimulation and movement onset

claims.claim: Approximately half (49.9 ± 14.2%) of all segmented cells in motor cortex responded to cerebellar stimulation
claims.source: Across all recordings and sites of stimulation the number of responders was roughly half of all segmented cells in motor cortex (49.9 ± 14.2%, mean ± SD, 2227/4614 cells, N = 2 mice).
claims.evidence: Quantification of responsive cells in motor cortex during cerebellar stimulation

claims.claim: Stimulation of Purkinje cells over both cerebellar hemispheres evoked opposing head movements with leftward movements when stimulating over left and rightward movements when stimulating over right crus II
claims.source: Stimulation of Purkinje cells over both cerebellar hemispheres evoked opposing head movements as determined from our accelerometer data with leftward movements when stimulating over left and rightward movements when stimulating over right crus II (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: Accelerometer data showing lateralized movement responses to cerebellar stimulation

claims.claim: NINscope can extract signals from up to 84 cells in dorsal striatum
claims.source: In DS, we extracted signals from up to 84 cells (62 ± 16.70, mean ± SD, range 38–84; Figure 5C), which, based on their calcium transients, had a rate of ~1 Hz (1.106 ± 0.93 Hz, mean ± SD, n = 308 cells, N = 5 mice) (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Number of cells extracted from dorsal striatum recordings

claims.claim: A majority of neurons (85%) in the right dorsal striatum had peak responses after left turn initiation
claims.source: During left turns (contralateral to the imaging location in DS), a majority of neurons in the right DS (85%, n = 308 cells, N = 5 mice) had peak responses after action initiation and 20% displayed significantly elevated responses for the duration of action execution (paired t-test baseline vs action execution activity, p<0.05) (Figure 5G,H).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of neural responses during contraversive movements

claims.claim: None of the dorsal striatum cells responded during forward-backward movements or movements ipsilateral to the site of recording
claims.source: None of the cells we recorded from responded during forward-backward movements or movements ipsilateral to the site of recording (Figure 5G,H), confirming lateralization of movement signals in the striatum.
claims.evidence: Analysis of neural responses during different movement types

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of orbitofrontal cortex resulted in 20% of dorsal striatum neurons showing decreased activity, 69% showing no change, and 11% showing increased activity
claims.source: Modulation of activity in subpopulations of DS neurons during OFC stimulation was observed: 20% of the neurons (26/133) displayed a significant decrease in activity, 69% displayed no change (93/133) and 11% (15/133) were increased.
claims.evidence: Quantification of dorsal striatum responses to OFC stimulation

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of secondary motor cortex resulted in 7% of dorsal striatum neurons showing decreased activity, 86% showing no change, and 7% showing increased activity
claims.source: M2 stimulation had a comparable, but weaker impact on activity of subpopulations of DS neurons with 7% of neurons (7/107) showing a decrease, 86% (93/107) displaying no change and 7% (7/107) of cells showed an activity increase.
claims.evidence: Quantification of dorsal striatum responses to M2 stimulation

claims.claim: The fraction of responsive dorsal striatum neurons during cortical stimulation significantly differed between orbitofrontal cortex (31%) and secondary motor cortex (14%)
claims.source: Although the fraction of responsive DS neurons (i.e. those showing a decrease or increase) during cortical stimulation significantly differed between OFC (31%) and M2 (14%) (chi-squared(1)=13.85, p<0.001), the average response for each category of DS neurons during stimulation was comparable (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of responsive neuron fractions between OFC and M2 stimulation

claims.claim: NINscope uses thinner optical filters (500 µm dichroic and excitation filter, 1 mm emission filter) compared to other miniscopes
claims.source: A thinner optical emission filter and dichroic mirror (both 500 µm) were used and the emission filter (1 mm) was glued to a plano-convex lens using optical bonding glue (NOA81, Norland Products).
claims.evidence: Specifications of optical components used in NINscope design

claims.claim: NINscope uses custom high-density interconnector (HDI) sensor and interface PCBs measuring 10 by 10 mm
claims.source: Custom high-density interconnector (HDI) sensor and interface PCBs (10 by 10 mm, Figure 1B) were designed, fitted with electronic components using a pick-and-place machine (NeoDen4, NeoDen Tech, Hangzhou, China) and stacked to maintain a small footprint.
claims.evidence: Dimensions and design of custom PCBs are specified

claims.claim: NINscope acquisition rate is set to 30 frames per second
claims.source: We set acquisition rate in the current NINscope to 30 frames per second and the frame size to 752 × 480 pixels to allow read-out of both pixel data and three accelerometer channels from the IMU.
claims.evidence: Frame rate specification for current NINscope configuration

claims.claim: Minimal light power of approximately 120-240 μW before entering the GRIN objective was required to obtain high quality signal-to-noise recordings
claims.source: For all recordings minimal light power (~120–240 μW before, 30–140 μW after entering the GRIN objective, well within the linear range of the excitation LED driver, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) was required to obtain high quality signal-to-noise recordings using a GRIN objective mounted on the brain surface (Figure 2D, Figure 2—video 1).
claims.evidence: Measured light power requirements for imaging

claims.claim: No signal bleaching or photodamage was observed for the duration of imaging sessions (typically 5,000-20,000 frames, 2-11 min per session repeated at least 10 times)
claims.source: No signal bleaching or photodamage was observed for the duration of our imaging sessions (typically 5.000–20.000 frames, that is, 2–11 min per session repeated with brief intermissions at least 10 times).
claims.evidence: Observation of signal stability over multiple imaging sessions

claims.claim: The inter-baseplate distance for dual miniscope recordings from cerebellum and cortex is approximately 8 mm at angles of 15-20°
claims.source: Our miniscope design allows recordings from two regions in mice with an inter-baseplate distance of ~8 mm and miniscopes placed at an angle of 15–20° in the case of concurrent recordings from cerebellum and cortex (or alternatively dorsal striatum, Figure 3C,D), and ~6–7 mm at an angle of 45–50° when placed side-by-side for bihemispheric recordings from cerebellum or cortex.
claims.evidence: CAD modeling measurements of dual miniscope placement configurations

claims.claim: Signals could be extracted from hundreds of cells in cerebellum (141 ± 53, range 62-200) and cortex (201 ± 90, range 89-361) during dual site recordings
claims.source: Signals could be extracted from hundreds of cells in the cerebellum and cortex (cerebellum: 141 ± 53, range 62–200, cortex: 201 ± 90, range 89–361, mean ± SD, N = 4 mice, Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Quantification of extracted cells from dual region recordings

claims.claim: Cerebellar Purkinje cells displayed significantly more within-region synchronous patterns than cortical neurons (lobule VI: 66.4 ± 18.9%, simplex lobule: 73.3 ± 27.4%, cortex: 35.7 ± 17%)
claims.source: Both cerebellar Purkinje cells and cortical neurons displayed SPs within and across regions, with Purkinje cells having significantly more within-SPs than cortical neurons (fraction of total lobule VI: 66.4 ± 18.9%, simplex lobule: 73.3 ± 27.4%, cortex: 35.7 ± 17%, mean ± SD, CBL vs CTX p=2.7801e-17, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of within-region synchronous pattern frequencies

claims.claim: Latencies to peak response of calcium transients in cerebellum (444 ± 280 ms) and cortex (505 ± 260 ms) preceded the peak compound acceleration signal (700 ± 269 ms)
claims.source: Latencies to peak response of the calcium transients in cerebellum, cortex and the compound acceleration signal revealed that the maximum acceleration came after the peak response in both cerebellum and cortex (CBL: 444 ± 280 ms, CTX: 505 ± 260 ms, axyz: 700 ± 269 ms, Kruskal-Wallis test p=1.6553e-08).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of temporal relationships between neural activity and movement

claims.claim: Mean amplitudes of Z-scored calcium transients in motor cortex neurons varied depending on the cerebellar region stimulated (crus II ipsi: 2.1 ± 1.3 Z; crus II contra: 2.9 ± 1.5 Z; lobule VI: 2.9 ± 1.6 Z; simplex lobule: 2.0 ± 1.3 Z)
claims.source: Mean amplitudes of Z-scored calcium transients measured in neurons of motor cortex varied depending on the region stimulated (crus II ipsi: 2.1 ± 1.3 Z; crus II contra: 2.9 ± 1.5 Z; lobule VI: 2.9 ± 1.6 Z; simplex lobule: 2.0 ± 1.3 Z; Kruskal-Wallis test p=1.1239e-70 and post-hoc multiple comparisons using Sheffe's S revealed significantly different mean ranks for stimulation of contralateral lobule VI and crus II relative to the other groups) (Figure 4G), but all displayed comparable onset times (crus II ipsi: 218 ± 120 ms; crus II contra: 221 ± 118 ms; lobule VI: 233 ± 123 ms; simplex lobule: 212 ± 130 ms, mean ± SD; Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.1, n.s) relative to stimulus offset.
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of cortical response amplitudes to cerebellar stimulation at different sites

claims.claim: The largest dorsal striatum responses began after movement initiation with a latency onset of 310 ± 45 ms
claims.source: The largest of these began after movement initiation, suggesting a predominant association with action execution rather than preparation (latency onset, 310 ± 45 ms, mean ± SD).
claims.evidence: Temporal analysis of neural responses relative to movement initiation

claims.claim: NINscope is an open-source project with design files and software available on GitHub
claims.source: NINscope is an open-source project enabling others to build on its design and functionalities, thereby contributing to a growing range of open-source tools to study neural circuits during unrestrained behavior.
claims.evidence: Statement about open-source availability of NINscope

claims.claim: The UCLA Miniscope v3 weighs 3.2 grams
claims.source: UCLA Miniscope v31	3.2	no	no	no	no	no	no	no	no
claims.evidence: Comparison table showing weight of UCLA Miniscope v3

claims.claim: Climbing fibers trigger calcium influx throughout the Purkinje cell dendrite arbor and their firing frequency is stably maintained at around 1 Hz
claims.source: Climbing fibers derived from the inferior olive in the ventral medulla elicit complex spikes in Purkinje cells; they trigger calcium influx throughout the Purkinje cell dendrite arbor up to the brain surface and their firing frequency is stably maintained at around 1 Hz (Ju et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Statement about climbing fiber properties with citation

claims.claim: Purkinje cell dendrites have a parasagittal arrangement, span up to ~150 µm in width, and have a thickness of ~4-6 µm
claims.source: The parasagittal arrangement of Purkinje cell dendrites, which each span up to ~150 µm in width and have a thickness of ~4–6 µm (Nedelescu and Abdelhack, 2013), make them amenable for miniscope imaging (Ghosh et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Anatomical description of Purkinje cell dendrites with citations

claims.claim: There is anatomical evidence for cerebello-thalamo-cerebral loops
claims.source: There is ample anatomical evidence for cerebello-thalamo-cerebral loops (Hoover and Strick, 1999; Akkal et al., 2007; Bostan et al., 2013) and an increasing number of studies suggest that functional interactions within such loops are important for the proper expression of social, cognitive and motor (planning) behaviors (Badura et al., 2018; Stoodley et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Statement about anatomical connectivity with multiple citations

claims.claim: Functional interactions within cerebello-thalamo-cerebral loops are important for social, cognitive and motor planning behaviors
claims.source: There is ample anatomical evidence for cerebello-thalamo-cerebral loops (Hoover and Strick, 1999; Akkal et al., 2007; Bostan et al., 2013) and an increasing number of studies suggest that functional interactions within such loops are important for the proper expression of social, cognitive and motor (planning) behaviors (Badura et al., 2018; Stoodley et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Statement about functional significance with citations

claims.claim: Disinhibition of Purkinje cells and associated rebound excitation of neurons in the cerebellar nuclei can elicit delayed motor reflexes
claims.source: The miniscope accelerometer data registered movement that occurred with a delay after stimulus offset (crus II ipsi: 76 ± 23 ms; crus II contra: 80 ± 30 ms; lobule VI: 79 ± 34 ms; simplex lobule: 73 ± 32 ms, mean ± SD, N = 2 mice) in line with earlier observations that disinhibition of Purkinje cells and associated rebound excitation of neurons in the cerebellar nuclei can elicit delayed motor reflexes (Hoebeek et al., 2010; Witter et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Interpretation of results based on cited previous findings

claims.claim: Crus I and II in rodents receive inputs related to orofacial and whisking behavior as well as head and neck information
claims.source: These data are in line with the findings that crus I and II in rodents do not only receive inputs related to orofacial and whisking behavior (Ju et al., 2019; Romano et al., 2018), but also head and neck information (Quy et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2013), and that activation of the cerebellar hemispheres in humans is associated with head movements (Prudente et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Statement about cerebellar inputs with multiple citations

claims.claim: Activation of the cerebellar hemispheres in humans is associated with head movements
claims.source: These data are in line with the findings that crus I and II in rodents do not only receive inputs related to orofacial and whisking behavior (Ju et al., 2019; Romano et al., 2018), but also head and neck information (Quy et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2013), and that activation of the cerebellar hemispheres in humans is associated with head movements (Prudente et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Statement about human cerebellar function with citation

claims.claim: The dorsal striatum plays a role in contraversive movement initiation and action encoding
claims.source: In order to validate NINscope to study the striatum in unrestrained animals and in particular to prove its effectiveness for deep-brain imaging, we revisited previous work that has proposed a role of the dorsal striatum (DS) in contraversive movement initiation and action encoding (Klaus et al., 2017; Cui et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Statement about dorsal striatum function with citations

claims.claim: Orbitofrontal cortex and secondary motor cortex can differentially regulate the activity of neurons in specific dorsal striatum regions in vitro
claims.source: The OFC and M2 can differentially regulate the activity of neurons in specific DS regions in vitro (Corbit et al., 2019), with the impact of OFC on DS being stronger than that of M2.
claims.evidence: Statement about cortical regulation of striatum with citation

claims.claim: M2 input to dorsal striatum was more diffuse than the projections of orbitofrontal cortex
claims.source: M2 input to DS was more diffuse than the projections of OFC, consistent with previous findings (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Corbit et al., 2019; Hunnicutt et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Anatomical observation consistent with cited literature

claims.claim: Imaging approaches can sample the activity of individual neurons and retain information about how their activity is spatially distributed in a large network
claims.source: While advances in electrophysiology now enable recordings from many thousands of neurons at once in awake animals (Juavinett et al., 2018; Jun et al., 2017), imaging approaches can sample the activity of individual neurons and retain information about how their activity is spatially distributed in a large network (Terada et al., 2018; Stirman et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Comparison of imaging and electrophysiology approaches with citations

claims.claim: An anatomical substrate exists for clustered activity in the cerebellum, where nearby Purkinje cells receive input from climbing fibers originating in adjacent neurons of the inferior olive
claims.source: Often an anatomical substrate exists for clustered activity such as is the case in the cerebellum, where nearby Purkinje cells receive input from climbing fibers originating in adjacent neurons of the inferior olive brainstem nucleus (Ruigrok, 2011).
claims.evidence: Statement about cerebellar anatomy with citation

claims.claim: Miniscopes have been instrumental in uncovering neural activity patterns during natural behaviors including social interactions and sleep with fully intact vestibular input
claims.source: Moreover, because of their ability to record in freely moving animals, miniscopes have been instrumental in uncovering neural activity patterns occurring during natural behaviors and related brain-states including social interactions (Murugan et al., 2017; Remedios et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2018; Kingsbury et al., 2019) or sleep (Chen et al., 2018; Cox et al., 2016) with fully intact vestibular input.
claims.evidence: Statement about miniscope applications with multiple citations

claims.claim: Open-source miniscopes have been used to probe cellular activity in rodents and birds during unrestrained behavior
claims.source: Open-source miniscopes are affordable tools to probe cellular activity in rodents (Ghosh et al., 2011; Cai et al., 2016) and birds (Liberti et al., 2016; Liberti et al., 2017) during unrestrained behavior and until recently have been limited to recordings from a single region, but see Gonzalez et al. (2019).
claims.evidence: Statement about open-source miniscope applications with citations

claims.claim: NINscope uses a low-power 3D accelerometer and gyroscope iNemo inertial module (LSM6DSLTR) with 0.65 mA current consumption in high-performance mode
claims.source: A low-power (0.65 mA in high-performance mode) 3D accelerometer and gyroscope iNemo inertial module (LSM6DSLTR, STMicroelectronics), set of LED drivers (single LED for optogenetic stimuli: LM36011; dual LED for one fluorescence excitation LED: LM3643, Texas Instruments) and I/O expander (FXL6408, ON Semiconductor) are controlled over the I2C bus.
claims.evidence: Technical specifications of the IMU component

claims.claim: The IMU accelerometer has a range of +/- 2 g where each bit corresponds to 0.061 mg with a sample rate of 104 Hz
claims.source: The IMU accelerometer has a range of + /- 2 g where each bit corresponds to 0.061 mg. A sample rate of 104 Hz is set, which fills a FIFO buffer with x,y,z data that are read out at the end of every image frame and transmitted over the virtual serial connection with the computer.
claims.evidence: Technical specifications of accelerometer operation

claims.claim: NINscope uses a single-LED flash driver (LM36011) for optogenetic stimulation and a dual-LED driver (LM3643) for fluorescence excitation
claims.source: A single-LED flash driver (LM36011, Texas Instruments) and dual-LED driver (LM3643, Texas Instruments) were used to respectively control the generation of optogenetic pulses in a 470 nm LED probe (LED 150040BS73240, 402 case size, Wurth Electronics) or 630 nm LED probe (APHHS1005SURCK, Kingbright) and a 470 nm fluorescence excitation LED (Excitation LED LXML-PB02 470 nm, Lumileds).
claims.evidence: Technical specifications of LED drivers and LEDs used

claims.claim: The optogenetic LED can be adjusted in increments of 11.725 mA and the excitation LED in 1.4 mA increments
claims.source: The optogenetic LED can be adjusted in increments of 11.725 mA and the excitation LED in 1.4mA increments.
claims.evidence: Technical specifications of LED current control

claims.claim: The thinnest functional wall of the final NINscope prototype had a thickness of 500 µm
claims.source: Microscope housing prototypes were designed using Inventor (AutoDesk) with initial prototypes being printed using a Micro Plus Advantage printer (EnvisionTec) using the RCP30 M resin to allow printing of fine detail. The thinnest functional wall of the final prototype had a thickness of 500 µm.
claims.evidence: Specification of minimum wall thickness in 3D printed housing

claims.claim: NINscope uses custom-diced optical filters including excitation (ET470/40 × 3.5×3.5 x 0.5 mm), dichroic (T495lpxr 3.5 × 5×0.5 mm), and emission filters (ET525/50 m, 4 × 4×1 mm)
claims.source: We used custom-diced excitation (ET470/40 × 3.5×3.5 x 0.5 mm, Chroma), dichroic (T495lpxr 3.5 × 5×0.5 mm, Chroma) and emission filters (ET525/50 m, 4 × 4×1 mm, Chroma), a N-BK7 half ball lens (3 mm diameter, 47–269, Edmund Optics) and a plano-convex lens (4.0 mm diameter, 10.0 mm focal length, 45–429, Edmund Optics) to focus onto the CMOS image sensor.
claims.evidence: Detailed specifications of optical components

claims.claim: NINscope uses a GRIN lens with numerical aperture 0.55 and 1.8 mm diameter as the objective
claims.source: The GRIN lens (NA 0.55, 64–519, Edmund Optics) was implanted for superficial imaging, or glued into the baseplate for deep-brain imaging, and the miniscope was mounted on a baseplate that was cemented to the skull.
claims.evidence: Specifications of the GRIN objective lens

claims.claim: NINscope firmware is based on Cypress application note AN75779
claims.source: The NINscope firmware is based on example firmware derived from the Cypress application note AN75779 (modification date: 30/10/2017).
claims.evidence: Source of firmware development

claims.claim: The CMOS image sensor is registered as a USB imaging device and expanded to function as a composite USB device with a virtual serial port
claims.source: The CMOS image sensor which is registered as a USB imaging device is expanded to function as a composite USB device to allow the addition of a virtual serial port.
claims.evidence: Description of USB device configuration

claims.claim: The virtual serial port is used for communication and configuration of the CMOS sensor and LED drivers as well as for logging of accelerometer data
claims.source: The virtual serial port is used for communication and configuration of the CMOS sensor and LED drivers (e.g. to set image sensor gain, brightness, black levels, LED settings, optogenetic stimulus parameters) as well as for logging of the accelerometer data.
claims.evidence: Description of serial port functionality

claims.claim: NINscope software uses ring buffers to avoid frame time delays and frame drops during acquisition
claims.source: Within the Processing sketch a capture event function transfers each captured image into a ring buffer for rapid processing of the image and to avoid long hard drive (HD) access times which could cause frame drops. A thread is used to save all images from ring buffer to HD. The size of the ring buffer can be modified in the sketch but is set to 60.
claims.evidence: Description of software buffering strategy

claims.claim: The last 4 pixels of each frame are reserved for a frame counter to monitor dropped frames
claims.source: The Last 4 pixels of a frame are reserved for a frame counter to monitor dropped frames.
claims.evidence: Description of frame counter implementation

claims.claim: Every frame is saved as a grayscale tiff image with the smallest possible header to reduce file size
claims.source: Every frame is saved as a grayscale tiff image with the smallest possible header to reduce file size.
claims.evidence: Description of image file format

claims.claim: Mice were housed socially in groups of up to five mice prior to GRIN lens implantations, after which they were housed solitarily
claims.source: Mice were housed socially in groups of up to five mice prior to GRIN lens implantations, after which they were housed solitary.
claims.evidence: Description of animal housing conditions

claims.claim: Mice were kept on a 12:12 hr light:dark cycle with lights on from 7:00 to 19:00
claims.source: Mice were kept on a 12:12 hr light:dark cycle with lights on from 7:00 to 19:00.
claims.evidence: Description of light cycle conditions

claims.claim: For cerebellar and cortical imaging, a GRIN objective lens (1.8 mm diameter, 0.25 pitch) was placed on the brain surface
claims.source: For imaging of the cerebral and cerebellar cortex, a GRIN objective lens (1.8 mm diameter, 0.25 pitch, 64–519, Edmund Optics) was placed on the brain surface.
claims.evidence: Description of GRIN lens placement for superficial imaging

claims.claim: For deep-brain dorsal striatum imaging, GRIN relay lenses with a diameter of 0.6 mm and length of 7.3 mm were implanted
claims.source: To access deep-brain region dorsal striatum, GRIN relay lenses with a diameter of 0.6 mm (length: 7.3 mm, numerical aperture: 0.45, Inscopix, CA) were implanted (AP: 0.2, ML: 1.5, DV: −3.1).
claims.evidence: Specifications of GRIN relay lens for deep brain imaging

claims.claim: AAV1.CAG.FLEX.GCaMP6f/AAV1.CMV.PI.Cre.rBG mixed 1:1 and diluted in saline 1:3 was used for cerebellar transduction
claims.source: The skull flap and dura were then removed and virus (Cerebellum: AAV1.CAG.FLEX.GCaMP6f/AAV1.CMV.PI.Cre.rBG mixed 1:1 and diluted in saline 1:3; Cortex: AAV1.Syn.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 diluted in saline 1:3, UPenn Vector Core) was injected at four locations.
claims.evidence: Description of viral vector preparation for cerebellum

claims.claim: AAV1.Syn.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 diluted in saline 1:3 was used for cortical transduction
claims.source: The skull flap and dura were then removed and virus (Cerebellum: AAV1.CAG.FLEX.GCaMP6f/AAV1.CMV.PI.Cre.rBG mixed 1:1 and diluted in saline 1:3; Cortex: AAV1.Syn.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 diluted in saline 1:3, UPenn Vector Core) was injected at four locations.
claims.evidence: Description of viral vector preparation for cortex

claims.claim: At each virus injection location, 25 nl of virus was injected once at 350 µm, twice at 300 µm and once at 250 µm depth at a rate of 25 nl/min
claims.source: At each location 25 nl of virus was injected once at 350, twice at 300 and once at 250 µm depth at a rate of 25 nl/min with a Nanoject II Auto-Nanoliter Injector (Drummond Scientific Company, USA).
claims.evidence: Description of virus injection protocol

claims.claim: The GRIN lens was lowered until it touched the brain and then lowered an additional 50 µm
claims.source: The GRIN lens was lowered using a vacuum holder placed in the stereotactic apparatus until the lens surface touched the brain and then lowered an additional 50 µm.
claims.evidence: Description of GRIN lens implantation procedure

claims.claim: For dorsal striatum access, a track was created using a 25G needle lowered slowly over 10 minutes, left in place for 10 minutes, and retracted at a constant rate of 0.31 mm/min
claims.source: To ease implantation and reduce damage to tissue above dorsal striatum, a track was created using a 25G needle. Using a motorized stereotaxic arm, the needle was lowered slowly over the course of 10 min, left in place for 10 min, and then retracted with the same speed at a constant rate of 0.31 mm/min.
claims.evidence: Description of tissue preparation procedure for deep brain imaging

claims.claim: 500 nl of AAVdj.hSyn.GCaMP6s or AAV1.hSyn.GCaMP6f was injected into dorsal striatum at a rate of 100 nl/min
claims.source: Virus was delivered by lowering a Hamilton syringe over the course of 4 min to inject 500 nl of AAVdj.hSyn.GCaMP6s (N = 2 animals, Figure 5, N = 4 mice Figure 6) or AAV1.hSyn.GCaMP6f (N = 3 mice, Figure 5) into the dorsal striatum at a rate of 100 nl/min after which the syringe was left in place to increase diffusion of virus (5 min) and subsequently retracted (5 min).
claims.evidence: Description of virus injection protocol for dorsal striatum

claims.claim: The GRIN relay lens was lowered into the dorsal striatum at a rate of 0.10 mm/min

results.result: NINscope is a lightweight (1.6 g), compact miniscope with integrated hardware features including a PYTHON480 CMOS sensor, IMU accelerometer, and LED drivers for optogenetics and fluorescence excitation, using custom PCBs and 3D-printed housing with optimized optical components.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C58 provide comprehensive technical specifications for NINscope's hardware design, including weight measurements (C1), sensor specifications (C2), optical parameters (C3, C4, C25, C57, C58), electronic components (C26, C52-C55), and mechanical design (C56). These specifications are internally consistent and represent direct measurements or manufacturer specifications of components used.

results.result: NINscope integrates an IMU for behavioral tracking, an LED driver for remote optogenetic stimulation, and cross-platform compatible acquisition software with features for real-time control and data logging.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 and C36 describe the integrated features and software capabilities, while C59-C64 provide technical implementation details. The software architecture using Processing language (C7) and firmware modifications (C59-C61) are well-documented with specific technical details about buffering strategies (C62) and data handling (C63-C64).

results.result: NINscope enables dual-site recordings in mice without significantly affecting behavior, with inter-baseplate distances of ~8 mm for cerebellum-cortex configurations, extracting signals from hundreds of cells in each region.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 demonstrate dual miniscope capability with statistical validation showing no significant behavioral impairment (p=0.7864 for rearing frequency, p=0.4244 for duration, N=4 mice). Claims C30-C31 provide geometric constraints and cell yield data (cerebellum: 141±53 cells, cortex: 201±90 cells, N=4 mice), supporting the feasibility of dual recordings.

results.result: NINscope enabled the first concurrent cellular resolution recordings from cerebellum and cortex in unrestrained mice, revealing that coordinated cerebello-cerebral activity precedes peak movement acceleration, with Purkinje cells showing higher synchronous pattern participation than cortical neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C15 and C32-C33 describe novel dual-region recordings with specific quantitative findings. Event rates match expected climbing fiber frequencies (C12: 0.62±0.39 Hz), synchronous pattern analysis shows significant differences between regions (C13: p=1.8409e-15, C32: p=2.7801e-17), and temporal analysis demonstrates neural activity precedes acceleration (C33: CBL 444±280 ms, CTX 505±260 ms, acceleration 700±269 ms, p=1.6553e-08). However, the claim of being "first" (C10) cannot be independently verified from the manuscript alone.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of cerebellar Purkinje cells evoked delayed motor reflexes (73-80 ms) and activated approximately half of motor cortex neurons, with response amplitudes varying by cerebellar region stimulated and lateralized head movements corresponding to hemisphere stimulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 and C34 provide consistent evidence for cerebello-cortical connectivity. Movement delays (C16: 73-80 ms, N=2 mice) align with cited literature on cerebellar rebound excitation. Cortical activation (C17: 49.9±14.2%, N=2 mice) and lateralized movements (C18) are demonstrated with accelerometer data. Response amplitudes (C34) show regional specificity with statistical validation (p=1.1239e-70), though the small sample size (N=2 mice) limits generalizability.

results.result: NINscope successfully performed deep-brain imaging in dorsal striatum, extracting signals from up to 84 cells that showed lateralized responses to contraversive movements with peak activity after movement initiation (310±45 ms latency).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 and C35 demonstrate successful deep-brain imaging capability. Cell extraction (C19: 62±16.7 cells, range 38-84, N=5 mice) and lateralized responses (C20: 85% of neurons, N=5 mice) replicate prior findings. The absence of responses to ipsilateral movements (C21) confirms lateralization. Temporal analysis (C35) shows action execution encoding, though the distinction between preparation and execution could benefit from additional behavioral controls.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and secondary motor cortex (M2) differentially modulated dorsal striatum neurons, with OFC stimulation affecting 31% of neurons compared to 14% for M2 stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 demonstrate differential cortical input effects on striatum. The quantification of response types for OFC (C22: 20% decreased, 69% no change, 11% increased) and M2 (C23: 7% decreased, 86% no change, 7% increased) shows clear differences. Statistical comparison (C24: chi-squared(1)=13.85, p<0.001, N=4 mice) confirms significant differences in responsive neuron fractions, consistent with cited in vitro findings.

results.result: NINscope achieved high-quality signal-to-noise recordings using minimal light power (120-240 μW before GRIN objective) without observable photobleaching or photodamage over extended imaging sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 describe imaging performance with specific power measurements and session durations (5,000-20,000 frames, 2-11 min per session, repeated ≥10 times). The light power range is well-documented and within the linear range of the LED driver (referenced to Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The absence of bleaching/damage is observational but consistent with the reported power levels and GCaMP6 properties.

results.result: Detailed surgical and experimental protocols are provided for GRIN lens implantation, viral transduction, and imaging procedures across different brain regions including cerebellum, cortex, and dorsal striatum.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C80 provide comprehensive methodological details including animal housing (C65-C66), surgical procedures (C67-C76), recording environments (C77-C78), and validation approaches (C79-C80). These are standard methods with specific parameters that enable reproducibility. The protocols are internally consistent and follow established neuroscience practices.

results.result: Calcium imaging data were analyzed using CNMF-E for cell segmentation with region-specific parameters, and synchronous patterns were detected using a finite rate of innovation algorithm with Epanechnikov kernel convolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 describe the computational analysis pipeline with specific parameters for different cell types (C81-C82: gSig and gSiz values), response classification criteria (C83: mean+2σ threshold), and synchronous pattern detection methods (C85-C87: τ=1, kernel steepness=0.1, threshold mean+2σ, minimum 5 occurrences). The methods are well-established with appropriate citations and clear parameter specifications.

results.result: The UCLA Miniscope v3 weighs 3.2 grams, twice the weight of NINscope.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 provides a comparison weight from a published miniscope design shown in Table 1. This serves as a benchmark for evaluating NINscope's weight advantage (C1: 1.6 g), though the comparison should consider differences in functionality and components between the two designs.

results.result: The manuscript contextualizes NINscope within existing knowledge of cerebellar anatomy, cerebello-cerebral connectivity, striatal function, and miniscope applications, citing relevant literature to support experimental design and interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C51 represent background knowledge and literature citations that provide context for the experimental work. These include established facts about Purkinje cell physiology (C38-C39), cerebello-thalamo-cerebral loops (C40-C41), cerebellar nuclei function (C42), sensory inputs to cerebellum (C43-C44), striatal function (C45-C46), anatomical projections (C47), and miniscope applications (C48-C51). The citations appear appropriate and support the experimental rationale.
